headline: Your crazyhouse rating (1376) is not your strength. It is the average of a strong slow player and a player who runs out of time.

sections.title: 1. The clock is costing you more than chess ever could
sections.stat: 1317 of your 3655 losses (36%) were pure time forfeits.
sections.body:
You lost on time 1317 times. That is not a chess problem, it is a format problem. Look at what happens as the clock shrinks:

- 30+0: 327 games, 3.7% wins, 89.6% lost on time.
- 60+0: 410 games, 12.7% wins, 72.7% lost on time.
- 180+2: 946 games, 35.5% wins, 24.1% lost on time.
- 300+3: 823 games, 37.2% wins, 6.9% lost on time.
- 600+5: 105 games, 51.4% wins, 1.9% lost on time.

The clearest evidence that time is the problem is the 982 unlimited-time games you have played against Lichess AI level 5, where you score 40.9%. That engine is far stronger than your rating suggests you should handle, and with no clock you handle it.

One correction to an earlier version of this report: your correspondence record of 93.5% over 139 games is real but flattering. 83 of those wins came from opponents who abandoned after a few moves; only 47 were games that were actually played out. The conclusion still holds, it just rests on the AI games and on 600+5 rather than on correspondence.

sections.title: 2. You get killed before move 25, not after
sections.stat: Games past move 45: 70.3% wins. Games ending in moves 10-20: 26.9%.
sections.body:
- Games ending inside 20 moves: 2557 games, 26.9% wins.
- Moves 20-30: 1700 games, 29.8% wins.
- Moves 30-45: 977 games, 46.9% wins.
- Past move 45: 360 games, 70.3% wins.

If you survive the opening you are the better player, by a wide margin. Your understanding is fine. What kills you is a fast, prepared attack in the first 20 moves that you have to solve from scratch at the board - which costs you both position and clock. This is why opening drilling matters more for you than for almost anyone else: it converts thinking time into recall time.

sections.title: 3. The mate is never the mistake
sections.stat: 931 losses by checkmate - but the losing move came 3 to 12 moves earlier.
sections.body:
The squares your opponents mate you on, in order: g7, g2, f7, f2, g8, e2, h7, e1, h8, f5. Mates on g7/g2/h7/h2/g8/h8 are your castled king being blown open with dropped pieces - almost 300 losses. Mates on e2/e1/d1/f7/f2 are your uncastled king getting a queen or knight dropped beside it.

But knowing the mating square does not help much, because by then it is over. So the Collapses tab now works backwards: for each of these games it finds the earliest moment where the position was still holdable and your move made it lost, and asks you to find the move that held. Those moments land 3 to 12 moves before the mate. In more than 40% of them the saving move was a drop - defending with a piece from your hand is the skill you are missing.

Note also that castling early does NOT help you (32.6% wins when you castle by move 7, vs 34.7% when you never castle). In crazyhouse castling often just tells the opponent where to aim. The fix is not 'castle sooner', it is 'count what he holds in hand before you commit the king'.

sections.title: 4. Your biggest technical gap: you under-use drops
sections.stat: In 28% of your blunders the winning move was a drop and you moved a board piece instead.
sections.body:
Engine analysis of 400 recent games found the pattern clearly:

- 28% of blunders: the best move was a DROP, you played a board move. Mostly missed knight drops (302) and pawn drops (259).
- 12% of blunders: you dropped a piece when a board move was better - usually an impulsive pawn drop (343 bad pawn drops).
- You reached a clearly winning position and threw it away 542 times in 400 games.

So the habit to build is a two-part question before every move: 'what do I have in hand, and where does it go?' followed by 'if I play this, what does he have in hand, and where does it go?'. Pawn drops in particular are your weakness in both directions - you play too many bad ones and miss too many good ones.

sections.title: 5. Two opening habits are costing you hundreds of games
sections.stat: You play ...Be7 in 255 games where ...Bc5 is far better, and ...Na5 in 178 games where it is nearly losing.
sections.body:
Running the engine over your actual repertoire found the same mistake again and again: you play the safe, standard-chess developing move, and crazyhouse punishes it.

- After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5, you play **5...Na5** in 178 games. The engine rates it -5.4 against -3.2 for 5...Bc5. In normal chess Na5 hits the bishop and is fine; in crazyhouse the knight goes offside while White drops pieces at f7.
- After 4.Nc3 you play **4...Be7** (148 games, -2.9) instead of 4...Bc5 (-1.1). After 4.O-O you play 4...Be7 (60 games, -2.3) instead of 4...Nxe4 (-0.6). In the Three/Four Knights, ...Be7 again (47 games).
- As White in the Sicilian you play Bb5 (37 games, +1.3) where Nc3 is +3.1.

One habit explains most of it: **you develop the bishop to e7, where it does nothing.** In crazyhouse the bishop belongs on c5, hitting f2. Fixing this single move covers over 250 of your games.

By opening name the worst results are: vs Alekhine 205 games at 22%, vs Pirc/Rat 96 at 24%, and 1.d4 as White 306 games at 25.2% against 1.e4's 36.7%. Stop playing 1.d4. Your Scotch (427 games, 39.6%), Philidor (49.7%) and Sicilian (46.1%) are fine.

plan.title: Change your time controls today
plan.body:
Stop playing 30+0, 60+0 and 60+2 entirely. They are 924 games of pure rating loss and they teach you nothing. Play 600+5 (51% wins), 300+5 (43%), 300+3 (37%). Avoid 600+0 - no increment is what kills you, and you score only 24% there against 51% at 600+5. Always take the increment.

Since Lichess no longer lets you start correspondence games in variants, the closest substitute is a long game against Lichess AI level 5, which has no clock at all. You already score 41% over 982 such games. Use those as your thinking practice and 600+5 as your rated play.

plan.title: 10 minutes of puzzles a day, untimed
plan.body: Use the Puzzles tab. Every position is from one of your own games, so you are fixing mistakes you actually make, not generic ones. There is no clock and no score - take a full minute per puzzle if you want. The app shows each position again days later, spaced out, which is how patterns stick at any age.

plan.title: Drill three opening lines until they are automatic
plan.body: The Openings tab is now an explorer, not a drill: at every one of your turns it shows the engine's top three moves with evaluations, marks the move you normally play, and lets you play any of them out to see why it works or fails. Start with 'Two Knights: 4.Ng5' and 'Two Knights: 4.Nc3', where your habitual ...Na5 and ...Be7 are costing you two full pawns.

plan.title: Work the collapses, not the mates
plan.body: The Collapses tab gives you the position several moves before each mate, while the game was still holdable, and asks for the move that holds it. This is the hardest and most valuable tab: it trains the thing you actually lack, which is noticing an attack one move before it becomes unstoppable.

plan.title: Play one long game a day and analyse it
plan.body: One 600+5 game, or one untimed game against AI level 5, played properly, is worth more than twenty bullet games. After it, run it through the Lichess analysis board and look only at the moves where you had a piece in hand and did not use it.
